knowledge_point.title: Calculating Flux Across a Rectangle Using Two Symmetry Properties

question.:question/problem:
![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186179647/images/flux-1.0.2-8c7428d2b40a578c2791-field.png)

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F=-x\,\mathbf i+3y\,\mathbf j$ and a square $C$ with side length $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds,
$$

where $\mathbf n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds
&=\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_1\,\mathrm ds+\int_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_2\,\mathrm ds\\
&\quad+\int_{C_3}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_3\,\mathrm ds+\int_{C_4}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_4\,\mathrm ds.
\end{aligned}
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-z7ii9jxi/17592186179647/images/flux-1.0.2-8c7428d2b40a578c2791-normals.png)

We compute this integral in two stages.

- First, consider the side $C_1.$ We have that $\mathbf n_1=\mathbf i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_1\,\mathrm ds
&=\int_{C_1}(-x\,\mathbf i+3y\,\mathbf j)\cdot\mathbf i\,\mathrm ds\\
&=-\int_{C_1}x\,\mathrm ds.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_1,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t)=1\mathbf i+t\,\mathbf j,\quad \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf j,\quad t\in[-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
-\int_{C_1}x\,\mathrm ds
&=-\int_{-1}^{1}1\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm dt\\
&=(-1)\int_{-1}^{1}\mathrm dt\\
&=(-1)\cdot 2\\
&=-2.
\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side $C_3$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
\int_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_1\,\mathrm ds=\int_{C_3}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_3\,\mathrm ds=-2.
$$

- Next, consider the side $C_2.$ We have that $\mathbf n_2=\mathbf j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_2\,\mathrm ds
&=\int_{C_2}(-x\,\mathbf i+3y\,\mathbf j)\cdot\mathbf j\,\mathrm ds\\
&=3\int_{C_2}y\,\mathrm ds.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_2,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t)=t\,\mathbf i+1\mathbf j,\quad \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf i,\quad t\in[-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
3\int_{C_2}y\,\mathrm ds
&=3\int_{-1}^{1}1\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm dt\\
&=(3)\int_{-1}^{1}\mathrm dt\\
&=(3)\cdot 2\\
&=6.
\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side $C_4$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
\int_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_2\,\mathrm ds=\int_{C_4}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n_4\,\mathrm ds=6.
$$

Finally, then

$$
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds=2\cdot(-2)+2\cdot(6)=8.
$$
